newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Milosevic rejects foreign pressure.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Milosevic rejects foreign pressure.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, in his first meeting with protesters in a crisis over annulled local election results, vowed on Tuesday not to bow to foreign interference in his country's affairs.

Milosevic, who has remained aloof from huge daily street protests which have shaken his administration, told a delegation of students in a rare meeting that his main task was to respect the will of the people and enforce the rule of law.

The students, who on Tuesday completed a 230-km (145-mile) protest march from the southern industrial city of Nis, appealed to Milosevic to abide by the law, shun dictatorship and resinstate the annulled results.

The official Tanjug news agency quoted Milosevic as telling the delegation: "A foreign hand shall not rule Serbia and we are our own masters in Serbia and we must resolve our problems within our institutions."

Referring to Washington-led international criticism of his handling of the elections, Milosevic was also quoted as saying: "Our country can be a good partner but should not be anyone's servant nor should it bend its head."
Predrag Cvjeticanin, who was in the three-man delegation, said: "We said for the past 30 days the people of Serbia have protested against the election fraud and he was not worried at all."
A court in Nis on Sunday told the city electoral commission to respect the outcome of November elections which handed significant victories to the Zajedno (Together) coalition.

"He (Milosevic) said he would do his best to make sure all electoral districts' results were legal and would punish all the guilty but he did not comment on the demonstrations in Belgrade or Nis or anywhere else," Cvjeticanin added.
The delegation also handed over a protest letter to Milosevic and what they said were spoilt voting records.

The student letter to Milosevic said: "With the wish that civil war never again breaks out in Serbia we remain determined not to allow dictatorship to take over in the country we live in, we call on you to return within the framework of the law."
There were 17 students on the march from Nis, one for each electoral unit they said was in question. They delivered copies of voting records for Milosevic to scrutinise for himself.
Tanjug said he sent them to the justice ministry to be investigated.
Supporters of Zajedno have been using marches across the country to spread their message, accusing the state media of failing to keep people informed about opposition demonstrations and aims.

Students have emerged at the forefront of protests at Milosevic's refusal to reinstate anulled November local elections and for the past four weeks have turned out daily in Belgrade and towns across Serbia to demonstrate.
